changelog: Insert a concise decision rule after C4 that allows noun+modifier cuts when forbidding them would force very-short (≈≤3–5 word) harmful splits, so scorers prefer preserving subjects/predicates; addresses the primary finding about an over-generalized ban on noun+modifier cuts.
findings: The prompt is over-generalizing a ban on cuts after nouns/specifiers: it treats most noun+postnominal splits as categorically harmful and so moves cuts elsewhere. That shift repeatedly forces very-short pieces (≤3–5 words) that split subjects, verbs, or internal compounds, which increases contradiction and cohesion loss in the short-latency bins.

The prompt underestimates the contradiction risk of leaving trailing adjuncts/ modifiers as standalone pieces (participial, prepositional, 'using...' phrases, 'in advance', 'and beyond'). Such trailing fragments often cannot be interpreted correctly on their own and create high contra when separated.

The prompt lacks short, concrete examples showing when to allow a noun+modifier cut to prevent worse subject‑verb fragmentation; scorers need a model example that trades a noun+modifier split for preserving a subject or predicate in very-short bins.

edits.now: Allow a noun+modifier cut when forbidding it would force other cuts into very-sh

diagnosis.why: Relaxing C4 to allow noun+modifier cuts when forbidding them would force very-short pieces caused the scorer to merge some noun+modifier spans but often pushed cut points onto small trailing complements or split predicates/prepositional attachments; that produced a small net drop in H_set, concentrated in the short-to-medium latency bins (≤3–≤10).
diagnosis.lesson: A later revision should respect that easing the noun+modifier ban to avoid tiny (≈≤3–5 word) pieces can reduce extreme fragmentation in some examples but must not systematically shift boundaries onto very-short trailing fragments or break predicates, since that harms short/medium bins overall.
